lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Polydeuces — listen, I've got an errand for you. The minute you go back up — it's your turn to come back to life tomorrow, isn't it? — if you happen to spot Menippus the Cynic — you'll find him in Corinth, around the Craneum, or at the Lyceum, laughing at the philosophers arguing with each other — tell him this: Menippus, Diogenes says, if you've had your fill of laughing at things up there, come down here, where there's a great deal more to laugh at. Up there your laughter still had a catch in it — you know, the whole 'who really knows what comes after life?' business. Down here you'll laugh without a shadow of doubt, the way I do now. Especially when you see the rich men and the satraps and the tyrants reduced to nobodies — you can only tell them apart by their whimpering — and what soft, spineless creatures they are once they start remembering the good old days up top. Tell him all that. And tell him to fill up his satchel before he comes — plenty of lupines, and any free meal he can scrounge at a crossroads, [pause] a Hecate's supper, an egg from some purification rite, whatever's lying around.
lines.description: brisk contempt, enjoying the logistics of mockery

lines.speaker: Polydeuces
lines.text: I'll pass it all along, Diogenes. But — just so I know him by sight — what does he look like?
lines.description: practical, mildly amused, taking the errand seriously

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Old. Bald. Wearing a little patched cloak with about a hundred openings in it — every wind goes straight through — a real mosaic of rags. Always laughing. Mostly at those pretentious philosophers.
lines.description: dry inventory, fondly scornful on the final phrase

lines.speaker: Polydeuces
lines.text: Easy enough to spot, from all that.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Would you mind taking a message to the philosophers themselves while you're at it?
lines.description: casual setup, as if adding one small errand

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Just — broadly — tell them to stop. Stop the babbling, stop the arguing about the universe, stop growing horns on each other and turning each other into crocodiles and teaching the mind to ask these impossible little questions.
lines.description: flat opening punch, then gathering irritated momentum

lines.speaker: Polydeuces
lines.text: Yes, but if I criticise their wisdom they'll say I'm an ignoramus with no education.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Then tell them, from me, to go hang.
lines.description: instant, clean contempt; no heat, just verdict

lines.speaker: Polydeuces
lines.text: Right. I'll pass that on too, Diogenes.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: And to the rich men, dear Polydeuces — give them this from me: You fools, what are you hoarding the gold for? Why are you torturing yourselves calculating interest, piling talents on talents, when you'll be turning up here soon with one obol to your name?
lines.description: withering sermon, controlled rather than shouted

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: And to the beautiful and the strong — to Megillus of Corinth, say, and Damoxenus the wrestler — tell them: down here there's no blond hair any more, no bright eyes or dark ones, no flush on the cheek, no taut sinews, no powerful shoulders. It's all just dust, as they say — bare skulls, stripped of any beauty.
lines.description: clinical dismantling, dry pleasure in each lost feature

lines.speaker: Polydeuces
lines.text: Not hard to deliver that to the beautiful and the strong either.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: And to the poor, Spartan — there are plenty of them, miserable about their lot, bewailing how little they have — tell them not to weep and not to wail. Describe the equality down here. Tell them they'll see the rich men of the upper world are no better off than they are. And while you're at it, if you don't mind, give your Spartans a piece of my mind too — tell them they've gone soft.
lines.description: unexpectedly practical, then sharp jab at Sparta

lines.speaker: Polydeuces
lines.text: Don't say a word about the Spartans, Diogenes. I won't have it. The rest of your messages, fine, I'll deliver.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: [sighs] All right, leave the Spartans out of it, if you insist. Just take the rest to the people I mentioned. From me.
lines.description: grudging concession, still needling under the sigh
